Question 1



Last week, you tested whether the average optimism score among DAPR1 students is greater than the general population average. You conducted a z-test to show that, yes, DAPR1 students are significantly more optimistic than the general population!
However, we don’t know the true population values for every variable, so we can’t always run z-tests. In real research settings, where we don’t know any of this information about the population, the kind of test we run is t-tests.
This week, you’re going to run some t-tests using t.test()! The cool thing about t-tests is that (unlike z-tests) you don’t need to know any information about the population at all.

This week, we’re going to look at the ampm variable, which ranges from 0 (total evening person) to 10 (total morning person). Here’s what that question in the survey looked like.





Our RQ is going to be: Do first year undergraduate students identify more as morning people or as evening people?
Read in the DAPR1 survey data from https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv.
In a one-sample t-test, we compare our sample to a specific value. Based on the RQ and the information above, identify the value that we want to compare our sample to.






TipHint





What value between 0 and 10 distinguishes evening people from morning people?
In other words, what value is the halfway point between someone being an evening person and someone being a morning person?








library(tidyverse)

sdata <- read_csv('https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv')

The value that distinguishes evening people from morning people is 5. People with ampm scores 0–4 are evening people, 5 is the midpoint, and people with scores 6–10 are morning people.
So we are going to compare our ampm sample to the value 5. This is the value that will appear in our null and alternative hypotheses.




Question 2


Based on the RQ, decide whether your alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) will be one-sided or two-sided.
Then, using the value you identified in Q1, specify the null and alternative hypotheses to address the research question.

🗂️ See the One-sample t-test > Define hypotheses flash card.





We’ll denote the mean “morningness” score of all first year undergraduate students as \(\mu\) or “mu”. (We’re calling it “morningness” and not “eveningness” because higher values correspond to higher “morningness”.)
We are testing the two competing hypotheses:
\[H_0: \mu = 5\] \[H_1: \mu \neq 5\]
To write these in plain text in your R script, you can write:

# H0: mu = 5
# H1: mu != 5

We have written a two-sided alternative hypothesis, because the RQ doesn’t specifically want us to test whether DAPR1 students are more evening people (which would be one-sided to the left, \(\mu < 5\)) or more morning people (which would be one-sided to the right, \(\mu > 5\)). The RQ just wants us to find out which direction the tendency goes, and so we have to leave both options open and write a non-directional, two-sided \(H_1\).




Question 3


Create a visualisation that presents the data in a way that is relevant to the research question.
There are lots of different ways you could do this—the choice is yours! Have some fun with it. Change colours, tidy up axis labels, etc.

🗂️ See the Plot a variable flash card.





Here’s one way, where the dotted vertical line shows the midpoint of 5 and the dashed vertical line shows the mean ampm score:

ggplot(sdata, aes(x = ampm)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = .5, fill = "darkblue") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(sdata$ampm), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Chronotype\n(evening person <–> morning person)",
    y = 'Count'
  )








Here’s another option that combines geom_density() with a new geom that draws a little tick up from the x axis when there’s an observation at that value: geom_rug().

sdata |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = ampm)) +
  geom_density(colour = 'darkseagreen4', fill = 'darkseagreen4', alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_rug(colour = 'darkseagreen4') +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = c('0\n(evening\nperson)', 2.5, 5, 7.5, '10\n(morning\nperson)')
  ) +
  labs(
    y = 'Density',
    x = '"Are you generally a morning person\nor an evening person?"'
  )








If you’re not sure about what a given line of code does, try commenting it out and running everything else to see what changes.




Question 4


Using a 5% significance level, perform a t.test() to test the hypotheses you specified above.

🗂️ See the One-sample t-test > Run the test flash card.






t.test(sdata$ampm, mu = 5, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)


    One Sample t-test

data:  sdata$ampm
t = -6, df = 133, p-value = 4e-09
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 5
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.98 3.95
sample estimates:
mean of x 
     3.47 






Question 5


Write it up!
To help, here’s the example write-up from the lecture:

To investigate whether the mean body temperature of all healthy humans differs from the commonly thought value of \(37^\circ\text{C}\), we performed (at the 5% significance level) a one-sample t-test of \(H_0: \mu = 37^\circ\text{C}\) against \(H_1: \mu \neq 37^\circ\text{C}\).
The sample results provided very strong evidence against the null hypothesis (\(t(49)=-3.14, p = .003\), two-sided). We therefore concluded that the mean body temperature of healthy humans differs from 37 and, with 95% confidence, is between \(36.69^\circ\text{C}\) and \(36.93^\circ\text{C}\).

Here’s how this same report might be written up in plain text in your R script:

# To investigate whether the mean body temperature of all healthy humans differs
# from the commonly thought value of 37C, we performed (at the 5% significance 
# level) a one-sample t-test of H0: mu = 37C against H1: mu != 37C.
#
# The sample results provided very strong evidence against the null hypothesis 
# (t(49) = -3.14, p = .003, two-sided). We therefore concluded that the mean 
# body temperature of healthy humans differs from 37 and, with 95% confidence, 
# is between 36.69C and 36.93C.





We wanted to find out whether DAPR1 students identify more as morning people or as evening people. To test this, we ran a one-sample t-test at the 5% significance level, testing \(H_0: \mu = 5\) (the midpoint of the evening-to-morning scale) against \(H_1: \mu \neq 5\).
On average, DAPR1 students in our sample differ significantly from this midpoint, with a mean score of 3.47 and a 95% confidence interval between 2.98 and 3.95 points (\(t\)(133) = –6.31, \(p\) < .001, two-sided). Thus, DAPR1 students identify significantly more as evening people.

Question 1



This workshop starts off conceptual again. The goal of the first part of this workshop is to show you where we get the \(\pm\) 1.96 multipliers that appear in the formula for a 95% Confidence Interval. Later in the workshop, things get more practical: you’ll use these multipliers to calculate a 95% Confidence Interval for your observed outlook scores.

Last week, you used replicate(), mean() and rnorm() to get estimated means from 1000 random samples from the population of outlook scores that we defined. This week, our exploration will start in a similar way, with a couple modifications.
First, our estimates will be more precise if we have more than 1000 samples, so we’re going to up this to 10,000. Second, we will set a sample size of \(n = 47\), the number of responses to the DAPR1 class survey. Each of the 10,000 means in means47 below is the mean of a different hypothetical sample of 47 students.
Copy and run this code.

means47 <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(n = 47, mean = 15, sd = 25)))







TipReminder/breakdown of how this code works





Let’s start with the innermost term:

rnorm(n = 47, mean = 15, sd = 25)

This bit of code takes a sample of size 47 from a normal distribution that has a mean of 15 and a standard deviation of 25.
(These are the parameters that we defined our population to have last week.) The result of rnorm() is a vector of 47 numbers. In our example, each number represents one person’s outlook score.
Next, by wrapping that whole bit inside mean(), we ask R to take the mean of those 47 numbers:

mean( rnorm(n = 47, mean = 15, sd = 25) )

Finally, by wrapping that whole bit inside replicate(), we repeat all of that however many times we want. In this case, we’ll repeat it 10,000 times. Each time, it takes a sample of 47 people’s scores (the rnorm() bit) and then finds their mean (the mean() bit). The result is a vector of 10,000 means.

replicate(10000, mean( rnorm(n = 47, mean = 15, sd = 25) ) )

Finally, means47 <- stores those 10,000 means into an object called means47.



Again, like last week, we want to use this list of numbers as a column of a dataframe. The code below accomplishes this, and does an extra step too: it sorts the values in the estimate column.
Specifically, the arrange() function in Line 4 takes the dataframe created in Lines 1–3 and sorts it in ascending order by the estimate column. After sorting, the first row contains the smallest estimate (i.e., the smallest sample mean), and the final row contains the largest estimate (i.e., the largest sample mean).
Copy and run this code.

data47 <- tibble(
  estimate = means47
) |> 
  arrange(estimate)

Now, answer the following questions:

What is the estimate in the 5000th row of data47?
Bonus conceptual challenge: Which measure of central tendency is given by the estimate in the 5000th row?


🗂️ See Subset a dataframe > Extract row(s) flash card.





There are a couple equally good ways to return the 5000th row of data47.



data47 |> slice(5000)

# A tibble: 1 x 1
  estimate
     <dbl>
1     15.0






data47[5000, ]

# A tibble: 1 x 1
  estimate
     <dbl>
1     15.0




The value that you see in your 5000th row might be different than mine. This is because when we’re drawing random samples, they’ll be a little bit different every time.
Now, as for what measure of central tendency this represents: Because we sorted this dataframe in ascending order and we’re looking at the middle value, 50% of the values will be smaller than the quantity in the 5000th row and 50% of the values will be larger. That means we’re looking at the median of all these sample means!

data47 |>
  summarise(
    median = median(estimate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 1
  median
   <dbl>
1   15.0






Question 2


Add a new column to data47 that contains the z-scored version of estimate. Name that column est_z.
Check that the mean of the new column is zero (or at least a very very small number close to zero) and that the SD is 1.
Copy and run the following code to create a density plot of your distribution of z-scores.

data47 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = est_z)) +
  geom_density()


🗂️ See Calculate z-scores flash card.





To create a new column called est_z containing the z-scored version of estimate:

data47 <- data47 |>
  mutate(
    est_z = (estimate - mean(estimate)) / sd(estimate)
  )

To check that it has a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1:

data47 |> summarise(
    mean_est_z = mean(est_z),
    sd_est_z = sd(est_z)
)

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  mean_est_z sd_est_z
       <dbl>    <dbl>
1  -3.34e-15     1.00


This number –3.34e-15 for the mean is written using scientific notation, which is a way to abbreviate very small or very large numbers. In this case, the number –3.34e-15 is very small: the e-15 bit means that the number contains a 0, a decimal, and then 14 more zeroes before we see the 334: 0.00000000000000334
This is very close to zero, so we are satisfied! (Sometimes R can’t handle actual zeroes, so it approximates zero using tiny tiny numbers like this.)
Finally, here’s the density plot of z-scores. Again, yours might look a little different because of the random sampling.

data47 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = est_z)) +
  geom_density()












Question 3


A 95% confidence interval (CI) contains the middle 95% of a standard normal distribution. In other words, in a standard normal distribution:

2.5% of the probability distribution is below the 95% CI’s lower bound, and
2.5% of the probability distribution is above the 95 CI’s upper bound.

We have approximated a standard normal distribution using these 10,000 z-scores. And we can approximate its 95% CI by taking the middle 9500 z-scores.
Extract two rows from data47:

the first row of the middle 9500 estimates, and
the last row of the middle 9500 estimates.

Answer: What are the z-scores in those two rows?






TipHint





If we have a list of 10,000 things, then the middle 9500 are between 250 and 9750.




🗂️ See Subset a dataframe > Extract row(s) flash card.





If we have a list of 10,000 things, then the middle 9500 are between 250 and 9750. So we want to look at rows number 250 and 9750.


Using slice():

data47 |> slice(250)

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  estimate est_z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     7.83 -1.96

data47 |> slice(9750)

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  estimate est_z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     22.2  1.95





Using square-bracket indexing:

data47[250, ]

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  estimate est_z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     7.83 -1.96

data47[9750, ]

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  estimate est_z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     22.2  1.95





If you want to get fancy, here’s a way to use slice() and square-bracket indexing to get both of those two rows in one command:



data47 |> slice(c(250, 9750))

# A tibble: 2 x 2
  estimate est_z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     7.83 -1.96
2    22.2   1.95






data47[c(250,9750), ]

# A tibble: 2 x 2
  estimate est_z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     7.83 -1.96
2    22.2   1.95





The lower multiplier is -1.96 and the upper one is +1.95.
As you see, these are close to -1.96 and +1.96, which is what theory expects for a 95% confidence interval. That’s cool!!
What this shows us: the multipliers for the 95% CI come from the z-scores that are at the lower and upper bounds of the middle 95% interval of the standard normal distribution.
The more samples we take (that is, if we increased our 10,000 to even more), the closer our z-scores here would get to -1.96 and +1.96.





Question 4


Now things are getting practical again!
Let’s use the \(\pm\) 1.96 multipliers to compute a confidence interval for the mean population outlook score, representing people’s pessimism vs. optimism on a scale from –100 to 100.
The formula for calculating the upper and lower bounds of the 95% confidence interval is
\[\bar{x} \pm 1.96 * SE\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean and \(SE\) is the standard error of the mean. \(SE\) is computed as:

\(SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\) if you know the population standard deviation \(\sigma\), or
\(SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\) if you only know the sample standard deviation \(s\).

First, read the data from the DAPR1 class survey (https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv).

🗂️ See Read in and inspect data flash card.

Next, using the formula above and our knowledge that the population standard deviation of outlook scores is \(\sigma = 25\): calculate the upper and lower bounds of the 95% confidence interval for the mean outlook score.





# Read DAPR1 survey data into R and store into an object called `sdata`
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv")

# Compute sample size (n) and sample mean (xbar)
n <- nrow(sdata)
xbar <- mean(sdata$outlook)

# Compute 95% CI
xbar - (1.96 * 25/sqrt(n))  # lower bound

[1] 17.6

xbar + (1.96 * 25/sqrt(n))  # upper bound

[1] 26.1






Question 5


Write a sentence interpreting the 95% confidence interval you just calculated.






TipHint





Check the lecture slides for how to interpret a confidence interval.







We are 95% confident that the true mean outlook score of all DAPR1 students is between 17.6 and 26.06.

Question 1



In this week’s workshop, you will practice transforming raw scores to z-scores, reasoning about the probability of those z-scores, and back-transforming z-scores onto their original scale. The goal of this workshop is to help you get comfortable with the concept of transforming variables into a standardised score.

Once again, read in the survey data from https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv. Store it under the variable name sdata.

🗂️ See Read in and inspect data flash card.

This week, we’ll work with the data about people’s outlook (how pessimistic vs. optimistic they are) and their chronotype (how much of an evening person vs. a morning person they are). Here are the questions that generated that data:





You’ll notice that each question uses a quite different scale: outlook ranges from –100 to 100, while ampm (the chronotype variable) ranges from 0 to 10. So someone with an outlook score of 10 is in a very different part of the scale, compared to someone with an ampm score of 10!
Create two new variables in your dataframe. One should be the z-scored version of outlook (call it outlookZ), and the other should be the z-scored version of ampm (call it ampmZ).

🗂️ See Mutate columns and Calculate z-scores flash card.






library(tidyverse)

sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv")

sdata <- sdata |>
  mutate(
    outlookZ = ( outlook - mean(outlook) ) / sd(outlook),
    ampmZ = ( ampm - mean(ampm) ) / sd(ampm)
  )






Question 2


In this question, you’ll find the pseudonyms, scores, and z-scores of the three most optimistic people and the three “morning people”-est people.
First, sort your dataframe by your outlookZ column, in descending order.

🗂️ See Sort a dataframe with arrange() flash card.

Next, extract the top three rows of your sorted dataframe.

🗂️ See Subset a dataframe > Extract row(s) flash card.

Finally, extract only the columns that we care about for this question: pseudonym, outlook, and outlookZ.

🗂️ See Subset a dataframe > Extract columns(s) > select() flash card.

Repeat this process for the ampm variable to find the three people who identify most strongly as morning people.
Is any of these people you?




Here’s how we’d do all of these steps, piped together into a single statement for outlook and another one for ampm.

sdata |> 
  arrange(desc(outlook)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook, outlookZ)

# A tibble: 3 x 3
  pseudonym outlook outlookZ
  <chr>       <dbl>    <dbl>
1 <NA>          100     1.70
2 mj            100     1.70
3 alex          100     1.70

sdata |> 
  arrange(desc(ampm)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(pseudonym, ampm, ampmZ)

# A tibble: 3 x 3
  pseudonym  ampm ampmZ
  <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>
1 <NA>         10  2.32
2 bartlett     10  2.32
3 <NA>         10  2.32







Question 3


From now on, we’ll just focus on outlook and its z-scores. *We’ll come back to ampm in the last workshop of this semester.)
Plot your standardised outlook scores (that is, outlookZ) as a density curve.

🗂️ See Make a density plot flash card.

Once you have made your plot, add this bit of code to the end of it. This additional code will overlay a red standard normal distribution (with mean 0, standard deviation 1) over your density curve. (The ...s in the code chunk represents the code you used to make the density plot.)

... 
  ... +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), colour = "red")







CautionRabbit hole: What do the parts of stat_function() mean?





You don’t have to know or remember any of this! But if you’re curious:

stat_function() adds a statistical function to the plot. This is different from adding a “geom” because geoms are based on data—statistical functions are calculated based on the information we give next.
fun = dnorm specifies that the function (fun) to add is the normal (norm) distribution (d).
args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1) specifies that the function should use a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, which are the parameters of the standard normal distribution.
colour = "red" tells R that we want the distribution to be coloured red.









ggplot(sdata , aes(x = outlookZ)) +
  geom_density() +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), colour = "red")













Question 4


This is a challenging question, get ready!
To start: Did anyone in your group give a pseudonym in the survey? If yes, use your groupmate’s pseudonym for this question; if no, use “noodle_horse” (that’s what Josiah calls his greyhound Dougal).
Next, extract the row containing that pseudonym from the dataset using the tidyverse function filter().

🗂️ See Subset a dataframe > filter() flash card.

Now: using the function pnorm(), compute the probability of seeing somebody less optimistic than this person. In other words, you want to find the probability that somebody has a lower outlookZ score than your chosen person (or greyhound).
Next: still using pnorm(), compute the probability of seeing somebody more optimistic than your chosen person (or greyhound).

🗂️ See Explore a normally-distributed variable flash card.

Finally: Check that these two probabilities sum up to 1.




Dougal the noodle horse is a little bit of a pessimist:

sdata |> 
  filter(pseudonym == "noodle_horse") |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook, outlookZ)

# A tibble: 1 x 3
  pseudonym    outlook outlookZ
  <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>
1 noodle_horse      -7   -0.629


For convenience, let’s extract his outlookZ value and save it under its own name.

dougalZ <- sdata |>
  filter(pseudonym == "noodle_horse") |>
  pull(outlookZ)

To compute the probability of observing a z-score that’s lower than Dougal’s z-score of -0.63, we give this z-score as an argument to pnorm() (see the flash card for helpful illustrations!).

pnorm(dougalZ)

[1] 0.265


There’s a 26.48% probability of seeing someone less optimistic than Dougal.
And on the flip side, to compute the probability of observing a z-score that’s higher than Dougal’s z-score, we subtract the output of pnorm() from 1:

1 - pnorm(dougalZ)

[1] 0.735


There’s a 73.52% probability of seeing someone more optimistic than Dougal.
These values do indeed sum to 1, and this should make a little bit of sense: for anyone else that you sample, they will either be more optimistic than Dougal or less optimistic than Dougal. So the probability of seeing someone either more or less optimistic than Dougal is 100%.





Question 5


Finally, z-scoring is not just a one-way process. Sometimes you might start with variables in z-scored form, and you might want to transform them back onto their original scale (in other words, you might want to “back-transform” them).
Here’s the process that will “undo” a z-score by back-transforming it onto the original scale:
\[
\text{value on original scale} = \text{original mean} + (\text{z-score} \times \text{original SD})
\] Here’s the more mathematical version of this formula from the lecture slides:
\[
X = M + (Z \times SD)
\]
where \(X\) is the raw score / the score on the original scale, \(M\) is the population mean (or our best guess about it based on our sample), \(Z\) is the z-score, and \(SD\) is the population standard deviation (or our best guess about it based on our sample).

First, to get the parts of this formula that we need, run the following code to find the original mean and SD of outlook and store them under their own variable names:

outlook_mean <- mean(sdata$outlook)
outlook_sd   <- sd(sdata$outlook)

Using the formula above, calculate the value on the original outlook scale that corresponds to a z-score of 1. (In other words, what value of outlook is one standard deviation above the mean?)
Finally, calculate the value on the outlook scale that corresponds to a z-score of –2. (In other words, what value of outlook is two standard deviations below the mean?)

🗂️ See Calculate z-scores > Back-transform flash card.





Back-transforming from a z-score of 2, the outlook score that’s one SD above the mean is:

outlook_mean + (1 * outlook_sd)

[1] 67.7



Back-transforming from a z-score of –1, the outlook score that’s two SDs below the mean is:

outlook_mean + (-2 * outlook_sd)

[1] -69.9

TipHints





Revisit the slides about different data types.








pseudonym (Name) is categorical (nominal), and it is the identifier variable.
birthmonth (Birthday month) could be thought of as categorical (ordinal) or categorical (nominal). If you thought ordinal, it’s because you thought that “January” comes before “February” in the calendar. If you thought “nominal”, it’s because it’s not really the case that “February” is better than “January”.
n_sibling (Number of siblings) is numerical (discrete).
spicy (Spicy food preference, in words) is categorical (ordinal).
spicy_num (Spicy food preference, as a number 1-6) is stored as numerical (discrete) data. However, this is a numerical encoding of a categorical (ordinal) variable, spicy. In other words, it’s the same information as spicy, just recoded as a number and the numbers are not really meaningful in themselves as they could also be recorded as 0-5 for example.
eye_colour is categorical (nominal).
distance_born (Distance between Edinburgh and birthplace) is numerical (continuous).
outlook (Optimism scale, -100 to 100) is numerical (continuous).
ampm (Morningness scale, -100 to 100) is numerical (continuous).
sleepqual (Sleep quality, 0-100) is numerical (continuous).
procrast (Procrastination scale, 0-100) is numerical (continuous).
multitask (Multi-tasking scale, 0-100) is numerical (continuous).
fav_color (Favourite colour) is categorical (nominal).
catdog (Preferred pet) is categorical (nominal).
threewords (Description of self) is categorical (nominal), and is a free text response so it’s rare for two different people to have the same answer.

Here is the basic code structure for taking a dataframe named mydata and adding a new variable (or changing an existing one).

Line 2 takes the data, and passes it to line 3.

Lines 3-5 “mutates” the data, adding a variable called new_variable. The new_variable is going to contain the values of an existing variable (old_variable) but with some function applied to them. For example, if we had new_variable = old_variable/2 then it would contain the same values but halved.
It feels odd, but it helps to think about the first line of code once we’ve thought of the others. This line re-assigns the name mydata to the mutated mydata, thereby making the change save to the object in R’s memory.


mydata <-
  mydata |> 
  mutate(
    new_variable = function(old_variable)
  )

To make a variable a factor, the function we want is factor(). This will consider every different value that we have to be a possible category:

factor(variable)

If we want to have a specific set of possible values, we can do so with the levels part of the function, replacing the "..." with the options we consider valid:

factor(variable, levels = c("...","...","...", ....... ))

title: W1: Introductions
text:
This week’s workshop is quite minimal. All we’re really wanting you to do is:

Explore the software and start playing around.

Meet some new people, make some new friends, and form a group to work with in these workshops.

From next week, you’ll be working in these groups collaboratively on the workshop questions, with one person doing the typing (the ‘driver’) and the others telling them what to type (the ‘navigators’). The role of driver will swap each week, so you’ll always get a turn at typing.


Question 1


The very first task here is to open RStudio.
R and RStudio is software that you can download and install on your computer, but for the duration of this course, we are providing you with a version on a server.
You can access the RStudio server by following the instructions on the FAQs page (see first drop down box).
We would recommend you bookmark the page so that you can easily find it again!




Question 2


The first thing to do is start using R just like a calculator.
Try doing some basic calculations by typing in the bottom left where you see the blue > and pressing enter.
Playing with these: *, /, +, -, ^ and seeing what happens - can you work out what each one does?






Tipstuck seeing a + symbol?





If we give R an incomplete request, then it will just stay waiting for it to be finished.
e.g., if we typed a query and missed a bracket, then R would just leave a + symbol to say “I’m waiting for more…”:

To get out of this we can either type the required stuff to finish the query, or, much more simply, just press the Escape key (Esc) on your keyboard and it will cancel the query and let you start it again.







Question 3


In order to save our work, we need to start writing our commands in a document. Something we can edit, save, come back to later on, and share with other people.

Open an R Script (File > New File > R Script).

A new window will pop up in the top left of RStudio. Write some calculations in there (put each one on a new line).

You’ll notice that writing in the script doesn’t actually perform the calculations. We need to “Run” the commands we are writing, which we can do by ensuring the cursor is on the line we want to run, and then either:

press Ctrl+Enter (or Cmd+Enter for Mac)OR
clicking the “Run” button in the top right of the R Script.






Question 4



# starting a line with a "#" turns it into a comment
# it means that R will not try to run it  

# we can store things in R's memory using "name <- value", e.g.:
my_name <- "Umberto"
about_me <- "Italian."
fun_fact <- "I can play the piano."

# this -- paste() -- is a "function". 
# it takes some inputs, and gives us outputs
# in this case, we give it a whole load of separate sentence fragments
# and it sticks them together: 
paste("Hello, my name is", my_name, 
      "and I am", about_me,
      "Fun fact:", fun_fact)


Copy-Paste the lines of code above into your R Script and edit them to provide some text about yourself (if you don’t want to share a fun fact about yourself, just share a random fun fact!)
Save your script (File > Save).
Close your script (there’s a little cross in the tab label at the top of the script)
Re-open your script (File > Open)
Celebrate!





Question 5


Finally, we’d like you to join your group on Blackboard Learn.
Groups are named based on the workshop (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and your table number.
So if this is Workshop 3, and you are sitting at table 6, you should join group “Group 3_06”.

Go to the course LEARN page
click Groups on the top menu bar.
click Workshops_1_2_3_4_5
Join your group
Now click on “Group Discussion Space” within the Quick Links folder of LEARN.
Upload your script to the discussion space, to share your fun fact with your group members.

text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. If everyone in the group has already had a week as the driver, start going round again!
The driver will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).

Open a new .R script, and load the tidyverse package.
Listen to your navigators

Question 1



This week’s workshop is a little bit more conceptual in nature. The steps that you work through here are not steps that you would use in an actual data analysis scenario. Instead, the goal is to help you get more comfortable thinking about the precision of a summary statistic like the mean.
Concretely, you’ll create your own sampling distributions based on a population we’ve simulated. And you’ll see that the standard deviation of those sampling distributions comes pretty close to giving the same result as the standard error formula you saw in the lecture! This tells us that the standard error is a reasonable way to calculate the precision of an estimate.

If our silly questionnaire was filled in by every person in the world, we would have billions of outlook scores that tell us how pessimistic vs. optimistic everybody in the world is on a scale from –100 to 100. That would be our population distribution. In real life, this is of course impossible, but for the exercises this week, we are going to imagine that we know the mean and standard deviation of the population distribution for outlook: the mean is 15 and the SD is 25.
Here’s what this imaginary population distribution looks like. (The numbers along the y axis use scientific notation: for example, 8e+08 means “eight followed by eight zeros”, or 800,000,000. These counts are huge because there are over eight billion people in the world!)









Now we are going draw samples from this population. We can generate a pretend sample of outlook scores by using the function rnorm().
Copy this code into your R script and (re)run it a few times. Is your fake sample and its mean different from ours? Is your fake sample different every time you run the code?

fake_sample <- rnorm(
  n = 5,        # how many data points do we want to sample?
  mean = 15,    # what's the mean of the distribution we're sampling from?
  sd = 25       # what's the SD of the distribution we're sampling from?
)
fake_sample

[1] -25.69  73.08  13.09  -5.96   2.75

mean(fake_sample)

[1] 11.5






Your numbers will look different to the ones below because of randomness in sampling.
One sample:

fake_sample <- rnorm(n = 5, mean = 15, sd = 25)
fake_sample

[1]  14.9  42.4  23.4  31.3 -11.8

mean(fake_sample)

[1] 20


Another sample:

fake_sample <- rnorm(n = 5, mean = 15, sd = 25)
fake_sample

[1] 21.63 21.60  2.13 39.38 -9.09

mean(fake_sample)

[1] 15.1







Question 2


You have hopefully noticed that every time we take a new pretend sample, the actual numbers it contains are different, and so is its mean. This point is key: the mean of each sample is a little bit different. This raises our next question: how different are those means?
To find out, we are going to take a LOT of samples from the population, find the mean of each one, and look at how spread-out they are. We’ll use the function replicate(), which lets us do something in R lots of times. Specifically, we’re going to draw and summarise 1000 samples.
Copy and run the following code.

means20 <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(n = 20, mean = 15, sd = 25)))

means100 <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(n = 100, mean = 15, sd = 25)))

Now, do your best to answer the following questions about this code (and ask a tutor if you’re not sure!):

What part(s) of this code draws a random sample from the population distribution?
Do all samples contain the same number of data points?
What part(s) of this code calculates the mean of the sample?
What part(s) of this code draws and summarises a sample 1000 times?
Which of these two objects, means20 or means100, has more variability among the means it contains?






The rnorm() bit, specifically: rnorm(n = 20, mean = 15, sd = 25) generates a random sample of 20 data points from our population distribution, which is a normal distribution with mean 15 and standard deviation 25. And rnorm(n = 100, mean = 15, sd = 25) generates 100 data points from the same distribution.
No: the first set of samples contains 20 data points each, while the second set of samples contains 100 data points each.
The mean() bit, specifically: mean(rnorm(n = 20, mean = 15, sd = 25)) computes the mean of the 20 randomly sampled data points.
The replicate() bit, specifically: replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(n = 20, mean = 15, sd = 25))) repeats the sampling-then-summarising process 1000 times, and it results in a vector of 1000 means.
There’ll be more variability in means20 than in means100. Let’s just look at the first six values (yours will be a bit different from ours):


head(means20)   # these means are more spread out

[1] 14.29 15.44  8.86  9.53 15.60 25.83

head(means100)  # these means are closer together

[1] 14.1 18.1 15.7 13.2 15.7 16.0


This result should make some sense: you saw in the lecture that bigger samples result in less variability among the means.





Question 3


In this question, you will prepare the two sampling distributions means20 and means100 for plotting.
Currently, means20 and means100 are both vectors. But ggplot doesn’t like vectors. It only likes dataframes, and so we are going to make two dataframes: one for means20 and another for means100. To make a dataframe, we’ll use the function tibble().
In the following code, replace the ... with the name of the appropriate vector. Then run the code.

data20 <- tibble(
  estimate = ...
)

data100 <- tibble(
  estimate = ...
)

The result should be two dataframes that each contain one column called estimate. In that column are the values that make up each of our sampling distributions.

🗂️ See Create a dataframe flash card.






data20 <- tibble(
  estimate = means20
)

data100 <- tibble(
  estimate = means100
)






Question 4


First, use ggplot to make two plots, one for each of these sampling distributions. What sort of plot? That’s up to you!

🗂️ See Plot a variable flash card.

Once you’ve made both lots, let’s display them side by side in the same graphic. To do this, we’ll need the patchwork package (and you might need to install it first!).

🗂️ See Use R packages flash card.

To arrange the plots side by side, you’ll need to:

assign each plot a name, e.g. plot1 <- ... and plot2 <- ..., and then
use + to place them side by side (plot1 + plot2) or / to place one on top of the other (plot1 / plot2)


🗂️ See Patchwork flash card.

Each of the plots shows “means from 1000 samples we might see”, which is to say, they each show a sampling distribution of the mean. Rememebr that, because each sample is a random selection of people’s outlook scores, the means of the samples were different (some samples were full of more optimistic people, some with less optimistic people).
Now, do your best to answer the following questions (and ask a tutor if you’re not sure!):

What differences do you see between the numbers in the plots you’ve made?
Bonus challenge: Why are the numbers different?






library(patchwork)

p20 <- ggplot(data20, aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram()

p100 <- ggplot(data100, aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram()

p20 + p100









On the left is the distribution of means from samples of size 20. These means range from just below 0 to just above 30 (we can tell from the numbers along the x axis). On the right is the distribution of means from samples of size 100. These means range from about 8 to just above 20—a narrower range.
There’s more variability in the means of smaller samples, and less variability in the means of larger samples. This happens because bigger samples are more likely to include a bigger part of the population, so their means should be a bit closer to the mean of the full population.






Question 5


The goal of this final question is to show you that the standard deviation of the sampling distributions of the mean is pretty darn close to the standard error of the mean that we calculate using the following formula:
\[
SE_{\text{mean}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
You saw in the lecture that the point of the standard error is to characterise “how much a sample estimate will vary due to random sampling”. And that’s exactly what our sampling distributions show as well! So it makes sense that they give us similar numbers.
Let’s see it in action. Here’s how we’d calculate the standard error of the mean, using our sample sizes of 20 and 100, our population mean of 15, and our population SD of 25:


\[
\begin{align}
SE_{\text{mean, n=20}} &= \frac{25}{\sqrt{20}} \\
\quad \\
&= 5.59 \\
\end{align}
\]

\[
\begin{align}
SE_{\text{mean, n=100}} &= \frac{25}{\sqrt{100}} \\
\quad \\
&= 2.5 \\
\end{align}
\]


Now, compute the standard deviation of the means from samples of size 20, as well as for the means from samples of size 100.
They won’t match exactly, but they should be close. And that’s why the standard error formula is so cool and useful! It lets us directly calculate how much sample means are going to vary, without needing to go through this long effortful sampling process.

🗂️ See Measure Variability > Standard deviation flash card.





There are a couple ways to find the SDs of these sampling distributions.
The first is using your original vectors means20 and means100:

sd(means20)

[1] 5.57

sd(means100)

[1] 2.47


The second is summarising the estimate column of data20 and data100:

data20 |>
  summarise(
    sd = sd(estimate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 1
     sd
  <dbl>
1  5.57

data100 |>
  summarise(
    sd = sd(estimate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 1
     sd
  <dbl>
1  2.47


Those numbers are indeed pretty similar to the SEs of 5.59 (for samples of size 20) and 2.5 (for samples of size 100)!
It’s really cool that statisticians figured out how to estimate the sampling variability using the standard error formula, because that save us from having to do all this sampling rigmarole. The standard error calculations above tell us how much the sample estimates will vary because of random sampling. So we can simply use the calculations to get at a theoretical probability distribution (the red curves below), rather than having to actually simulate stuff every single time.

Question 1



This week, we’re going to bring together many of the ideas we covered over the last few weeks and go step-by-step through the process of performing a null hypothesis significance test (NHST).

We start with a research question:

Research Question: Are first year undergraduate students more optimistic than adults in general?
Operationalisation: We surveyed students on a first year undergraduate statistics course (that’s you!), and asked them to indicate their level of pessimism/optimism on a sliding scale from -100 (pessimist) to +100 (optimist). Previous research using this measure suggests that the overall adult population has an average score of 15 and standard deviation of 25.
Data: https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv

Define the null and alternative hypotheses. (Check the lecture slides for guidance!)




The symbol \(\mu\) will denote the mean optimism score of all adults (i.e. the population mean).
We are testing the two competing hypotheses:
\[H_0: \mu = 15\]
\[H_1: \mu > 15\]




Question 2


In future, we’re going to learn and use functions in R that do all the steps of NHST for us. But for this week we’re going to break down the process, so you can see every step. That means we’re going to need a few pieces of information.
We’re going to need:

the size of our sample (that is, how many observations we have in our dataset), \(n\)
the mean outlook score that we observe in our sample, \(M\)
the hypothesised value that we are comparing our sample mean to, \(\mu\)
how much we expect samples of the same size as ours to vary

Figure out each of these values.






TipHints





You’ll need to read in the data using read_csv() first.
“How much we expect samples of the same size as ours to vary” is the standard error, as you saw last week. The formula is \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\) (or \(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\) if the population standard deviation is unknown). In this case, we are told that the population standard deviation is 25, so \(\sigma = 25\). And \(n\) is the quantity you work out in (a).








library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv")

# the size of our sample (that is, how many observations we have in our dataset)
n <- nrow(sdata)
n

[1] 134

# the mean outlook score that we observe in our sample
xbar <- mean(sdata$outlook)
xbar

[1] 21.8

# the hypothesised value that we are comparing our sample mean to
mu <- 15

# how much we expect samples of the same size as ours to vary (i.e., the standard error)
sigma <- 25
SE <- sigma / sqrt(n)
SE

[1] 2.16






Question 3


We use all the information from the previous question allow us to build up a picture of “what would sample means be like if the null hypothesis \(H_0\) were true”.
Based on that picture, we can calculate the probability of seeing a sample mean at least as extreme as the one we have seen, if the null hypothesis were true.
Here’s a visual way of thinking about the key parts of NHST:








Figure 1: Null hypothesis significance testing in a nutshell. SE stands for ‘standard error’.





Our goal for the next two questions is to figure out exactly how much area is in those shaded red regions in the tails of our distribution.
To do this, first we’ll need to convert our mean into a “test statistic”, which measures the distance between our sample mean and the hypothesised population mean in terms of how much we expect sample means to vary.
In this case, the test statistic is the z-score or z-statistic, because we’re comparing our observed mean to the distribution of means from all the possible samples we could have taken.
Using the formula below and the values you figured out above, calculate Z.
\[
Z = \frac{M - \mu}{SE}
\]





zstat <- (xbar - mu) / SE
zstat

[1] 3.16






Question 4


Now that we have our test statistic, we can calculate the corresponding “p-value”.
A p-value is the probability of seeing a sample mean at least as extreme as the one we have seen, if the null hypothesis were true. It corresponds to one, or both, of the shaded red areas in Figure 1, depending on how we phrased \(H_1\). (See the Hint below for more detail on this!)
Z-statistics are follow a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1, which is called the “standard normal distribution”. To work out the area of the standard normal distribution that’s on the appropriate side of our z-statistic, we can use our old friend pnorm().
Using pnorm(), figure out how much of the area under the standard normal distribution is beyond your z-statistic, in the direction corresponding to your \(H_1\).






TipHint





The direction of the area you’ll need to find is always the same as the direction of \(H_1\):

If \(H_1\) includes the > (“greater than”) symbol, then you need to find the area to the right of your z-statistic.
If \(H_1\) includes the < (“less than”) symbol, then you need to find the area to the left of your z-statistic.
If \(H_1\) is two-sided, then you need to find the area on the side that the z-statistic is closest to (e.g., if your z-statistic is positive, find the area to the right), and then double that value to account for both tails of the distribution.





🗂️ See Explore a normally-distributed variable flash card.





As our \(H_1\) states that \(\mu > 15\), we need to find the area to the right of our z-statistic.
By default, pnorm() will give us the area to the left. So to get the opposite of that, we subtract the outcome of pnorm() from 1.

1 - pnorm(zstat)

[1] 0.000784


The probability of observing a z-statistic like ours or even more positive, assuming the true population mean were 15, is .000784, or 0.078%. Very unlikely!







Question 5


Do your best to fill in the blanks in the APA-style report below:
Let \(\mu\) denote the (1)__________. At the 5% significance level, we performed a one sample z-test of (2)____ against (3)____. The sample mean (4)__________ (M = (5)____, SD = (6)____) was (7)__________ (z = (8)____, p (9)____, (10)____).
Check the lecture slides for guidance, and ask a tutor if you’re unsure!





mean optimism score of all adults
\(H_0: \mu = 15\) (in your R script, you can write H0: mu = 15)
\(H_1: \mu > 15\) (in your R script, you can write H1: mu > 15)
optimism score of first year undergraduate students
21.83
45.86
significantly higher than the mean optimism score of all adults
3.16
< .001
one-sided

Here’s the whole thing:
Let \(\mu\) denote the mean optimism score of all adults. At the 5% significance level, we performed a one sample z-test of \(H_0: \mu = 15\) against \(H_1: \mu > 15\). The sample mean optimism score of first year undergraduate students (M = 21.83, SD = 45.86) was significantly higher than the mean optimism score of all adults (z = 3.16, p < .001, one-sided).
